query: What additive manufacturing strategy and post-processing route can enable the fabrication of a refractory high-entropy alloy family (Group IV-V transition metals) capable of retaining high-temperature structural integrity, and what specific microstructural state is hypothesized to optimize mechanical performance while mitigating the inherent brittleness associated with interstitial impurities?

generation.hypothesis: Fabrication of a Group IV-V refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., HfMoTaTiZr or TaNbHfZrTi) via Selective Laser Melting (SLM) or Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using mixed elemental powders, followed by a high-temperature vacuum annealing post-processing route, can enable high-temperature structural integrity. The hypothesized optimal microstructural state is a single-phase BCC solid solution with a controlled, low concentration of interstitial impurities (O, N < 0.5 at.%) to mitigate inherent brittleness while leveraging Snoek-type damping mechanisms for enhanced energy dissipation and ductility at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Mixed elemental powder of Group IV (Hf, Ti, Zr) and V (Nb, Ta, Mo, V) refractory metals, with inherent interstitial impurities (O, N) typically < 0.5 at.% from powder processing.
generation.intervention: Additive manufacturing via Selective Laser Melting (SLM) or Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using mixed elemental powders, followed by high-temperature vacuum annealing (e.g., 1000-1400°C) to relieve residual stresses and homogenize the microstructure.
generation.conditions: High-temperature service environment (up to 800-1000°C), vacuum or inert atmosphere during processing to minimize further interstitial uptake, and controlled cooling rates to maintain single-phase BCC structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Single-phase BCC solid solution with a severely distorted lattice and high configurational entropy, where interstitial atoms (O, N) occupy octahedral sites, inducing Snoek-type relaxation peaks at elevated temperatures.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy and lattice distortion impede dislocation motion and atomic switches, raising activation temperatures for Snoek damping. Controlled interstitial content enhances damping capacity and energy dissipation without inducing excessive brittleness, while annealing relieves processing-induced stresses and promotes a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Retention of high yield strength (>1000 MPa) and improved ductility (>10-20%) at elevated temperatures (up to 800°C), with enhanced damping capacity (tanδ > 0.02) and resistance to thermal degradation compared to conventionally processed refractory HEAs.
generation.baseline: Conventionally cast or arc-melted refractory HEAs, which often suffer from inherent brittleness due to interstitial impurities and lack of microstructural homogeneity, leading to poor high-temperature ductility and structural integrity.
generation.boundary: Applicable to equiatomic or near-equiatomic Group IV-V refractory HEAs with BCC crystal structure. Not applicable to alloys with significant intermetallic phase formation or excessive interstitial content (>1 at.% O/N) which may induce embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal annealing temperature and time window for stress relief without grain coarsening or phase decomposition is uncertain. The long-term stability of the single-phase BCC structure under prolonged high-temperature exposure and cyclic loading requires further validation. The precise role of interstitial impurities in balancing damping and ductility may vary with specific alloy compositions.
generation.falsification_experiment: Fabricate HfMoTaTiZr HEA via SLM with and without post-annealing. Measure tensile properties (yield strength, ductility) and damping capacity at 25°C and 800°C. If annealing does not improve ductility or if interstitial content >0.5 at.% causes embrittlement, the hypothesis is falsified. Additionally, if phase decomposition occurs after annealing, the single-phase BCC assumption is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

The bcc HEAs, comprising group IV (Ti, Zr, Hf) and V (V, Nb, Ta) refractory elements, exhibit superior mechanical properties ( [22] – [26] ). These materials are attractive for optimizing damping response because their constituents have high solubility of both oxygen and nitrogen (˃5.0 at %) ( [27] ). The actual impurity concentrations are very close to the target, indicating that the addition of TiO 2 and TiN as a resource of oxygen and nitrogen is reliable in this study. It should be noted that even in the base HEA, the level of oxygen is 0.377 at %, resulting from the fabrication process.

High entropy alloys and related compositions are a relatively young concept for designing alloys. The formation of such multi component alloys was reported independently by Cantor et al. [ [1] ] and the research group around J.-W. Yeh in 2004 [ [2] , [3] , [4] ]. In contrast to most conventional alloys, high entropy alloys do not possess a single main alloying element but comprise a composition of multiple principal elements. The exact definition of high entropy alloys varies from source to source. The most common definition includes alloys consisting of at least five elements with a concentration between 5% and 35% each [ [5] ]. Other definitions demand a configurational entropy of at least 1.5 R [ [6] ]. However, both definitions are overlapping in large parts. Additionally, further criterions like the formation of a single phase solid solution were suggested [ [7] ]. These definitions are discussed extensively in recent review papers [ [7] ] and books [ [6] , [8] ]. The focus of the present work lies on the alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 , which is considered a high entropy alloy in agreement with all these criterions. Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
